title: A Device-Lending Program: Article and Fact Sheet
text:
NEWS ARTICLE - District Expands Laptop Lending After Pilot

The Riverton school district is considering expanding a laptop-lending program from two high schools to all six. During last semester's pilot, 320 students borrowed devices for at least one week. District records show that 71 percent of borrowers had previously reported sharing a home computer or relying mainly on a phone for school assignments. Technology director Amara Singh says the pilot suggests that device lending reaches many students with limited computer access.

The district also tracked repair and return problems. Twenty-eight devices required repair during the semester, and nine were returned more than two weeks late. Singh argues that these rates are manageable but says expansion would require a larger repair reserve and clearer replacement rules.

FACT SHEET - What the Pilot Did and Did Not Measure

- 320 students borrowed a laptop.
- 227 borrowers had reported limited computer access before the pilot.
- 28 loaned devices required repair.
- 9 devices were returned more than two weeks late.
- The district did NOT compare course grades of borrowers with non-borrowers.
- The district did NOT measure whether students completed more assignments because of the laptops.
- Student survey: 82 percent of borrowers said the device made it easier to complete schoolwork at home.

BOARD COMMENT - Member Rachel Moore

“The pilot proves that giving every student a laptop will raise grades. Eighty-two percent said schoolwork became easier, so academic performance must have improved. We should buy enough devices for every student immediately.”

BOARD COMMENT - Member Isaac Bell

“The pilot gives good evidence that the program improves access, because most borrowers previously had limited computer access and many reported easier home schoolwork. It does not yet prove an effect on grades. I support expanding the loan pool while adding assignment-completion and course-performance measures so we can test that stronger claim.”

The finance office adds another question: expansion would require not only purchasing devices but also budgeting for repairs, chargers, and replacement units. It estimates that the pilot repair rate, if repeated at a larger scale, would require a dedicated annual maintenance reserve. Singh says this does not weaken the access evidence, but it matters to the separate claim that district-wide expansion is affordable. Bell agrees and proposes reporting access outcomes and program costs separately so the board does not treat evidence for one claim as proof of the other.
